newsitem.title: INDIA: India's low-caste messiah falls from pinnacle.
newsitem.headline: India's low-caste messiah falls from pinnacle.

text.p: Laloo Prasad Yadav, the focus of a major corruption scandal in India, has fallen from the status of hero he acquired during a student movement that challenged a state of emergency in 1975.
For two decades, the 49-year-old leader from the eastern Indian state of Bihar reigned as a low-caste radical riding a modern democratic system to defy a centuries-old Hindu hierarchy.

But a corruption case which forced him to resign as the chief minister of his backward state, India's second most populous, has attracted charges which have made him much less of a prime ministerial candidate than he was once seen as.
Yadav resigned last Friday as federal police received a court warrant to arrest him in the $280 million scandal involving the suspected embezzlement of animal welfare funds.
Yadav says he is innocent and had refused to resign from office since April when federal police charged him in the case.

He rose to fame during a two-year emergency when he was jailed in June 1975 by the government of then Prime Ministe Indira Gandhi under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA). He named his eldest daughter Misa in memory of his detention.
Yadav was then a key member of a student movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan, a social activist.
When he was freed in 1977 Yadav became a lower-house lawmaker in the federal parliament. Newspapers then noted he did not have enough money to buy himself a train ticket to New Delhi.

As a member of a socialist movement spearheading job quotas in government for lower Hindu castes, Yadav, who belongs to a backward community of milkmen, rose to prominence in the then Janata Party, which split several times later.

"They are angry that I have acquired a passion for riding helicopters," the charismatic leader told an election rally last year. "Some upper caste people think cowherds do not deserve to fly in these imported machines," he complained.
In March 1990, Yadav rode to power as the chief minister of Bihar at the crest of a huge wave of low-caste support.
But he faced criticism led by the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party which accused him of encouraging corruption and caste friction by promoting the interests of his own Yadav kin.
He was seen as a front-runner for prime ministership ahead of general elections in 1996.

But his party fared poorly in Bihar compared with earlier elections and H.D. Deve Gowda from the southern Karnataka state emerged as leader in the Janata Dal-led United Front coalition that formed the federal government last June.
The coalition changed its leader to Inder Kumar Gujral in April this year.

Meanwhile, Yadav also faced a leadership challenge from fellow caste man Sharad Yadav in the party's presidential elections. On July 5, Laloo Yadav formed the breakaway Rashtriya Janata Dal saying there had been irregularities in the party poll in which Sharad Yadav emerged winner.
Around the same time, the federal police closed in on him in the "fodder" scandal case. His refusal to resign and face trial in the case left many of his allies in confusion.
"Has the CBI (Central Bureau of Investigation) made me chief minister that I should resign?" Yadav said several times.
Even as he quit last week, Yadav named his inexperienced wife, Rabri Devi, as his successor, angering critics.
For many Indians Laloo Yadav is a symbol of arrogance and corruption. But his followers see him as a messiah.

His typical audience includes the cobbler or "chamar" caste, regarded as untouchables in the Hindu system, Moslem weavers, cowherds, poor peasants and an ethnic group of "moosahars" who live by trapping field mice and sometimes even eating them.
Yadav, who has seven daughters and two sons, has been criticised for being a poor example in a nation of 950 million people trying to control population growth.
